source.title: Expand Neurons, Not Parameters
source.authors: Linghao Kong; Inimai Subramanian; Yonadav G. Shavit; Micah Adler; Dan Alistarh; N. Shavit

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. The abstract heading is blank, but the abstract text and the main paper and appendices are included.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly measures interference-related properties and tests whether redistributing a fixed parameter budget across more neurons changes them, using methods different from the original neuron-visualization examples.
record.gate_note: The study reports its own measures of feature capacity, neuron cosine similarity, clause collisions, and clause-structure recovery, as well as performance after fixed-parameter expansion. It cites prior polysemantic-neuron examples but those cited findings are not rows. It does not test individual natural-image neurons for responses to unrelated inputs.
record.test_reason: The study measures feature capacity (Scherlis et al.), which the authors treat as an inverse polysemanticity metric, in trained Boolean DNF networks. It varies the ratio of features to neurons and widens networks at a fixed non-zero parameter count. These results bear on V3 (sharing tracks feature-to-neuron pressure) and on V5 (an architecture change lowers sharing without hurting accuracy). It does not look at individual neurons' responses to unrelated inputs. Accuracy-only and cosine-similarity results are the study's own method performance or proxy constructs.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state that clause-aligned splits reduce polysemanticity metrics in Boolean tasks, and that the gains come from reduced collisions rather than precise feature assignment. They present this as consistent with the superposition hypothesis and as a proof of concept limited to small models.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses fixed-parameter neuron expansion: it duplicates trained neurons, partitions or randomly masks their incoming weights, prunes to maintain the non-zero parameter budget, and fine-tunes. It does not reproduce the original circuit-visualization or SoLU methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported gains vary with neuron count and feature demand: they tend to be larger for narrower models or higher clause/class demand and diminish as the dense model has more capacity. Clause-aware splitting usually performs best in Boolean tasks, while in the fixed-representation vision experiments it is only comparable to random splitting. Earlier FPE application gives the best final accuracy in the reported timing sweep.

fits_no_version.finding: Fixed-parameter expansion lowers mean cosine similarity between neuron weight vectors in Boolean and CIFAR-100 CLIP classifiers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Widening at fixed parameter count makes neuron weight vectors more orthogonal (a geometric interference proxy).

fits_no_version.finding: FPE raises CIFAR-100 CLIP classifier accuracy over dense baselines, with gains shrinking as width grows.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Redistributing a fixed non-zero parameter budget across more neurons improves accuracy in interference-limited regimes.

fits_no_version.finding: Theory: random sparse expansion cuts expected clause collisions by about α^-(2k-1) while preserving coverage.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Random sparse widening reduces expected feature collisions per neuron.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 306, 2026 (stated in the paper text)
record.problems: The paper says experiments focus on small, controlled settings and that extending to transformer-scale models remains future work. Real-data feature splitting uses approximate heuristics rather than true feature decompositions. Some mechanistic results are described as preliminary and are given only in figures without numerical values. The real-world analyses rely on proxies such as cosine similarity and Gram-matrix clustering rather than direct tests of individual neurons' input selectivity.
record.rows_left_out: Raw accuracy results for other datasets and settings—including FashionMNIST, ImageNet-100, ImageNet-1k, jointly learned CNN/Boolean representations, depth sweeps, structured sparsity, and DropConnect comparisons—are not separately rowed here because they do not themselves measure polysemanticity or an interference metric. Their general trends are summarized in the paper, but the direct interference and CIFAR-100 performance rows needed for the tested versions are retained.

untested.parts: No individual image-classifier neurons are examined for responses to unrelated inputs.
No transformer language models; authors leave transformers to future work.
Only single-hidden-layer Boolean DNF toy networks carry polysemanticity measures. There is no direct neuron-level selectivity measure, and no evidence from real vision or language models.
Not tested directly. Initialization, regularization and noise are not varied.
No activation-function (SoLU) or regularization comparison, and no polysemanticity metric on the real vision models. Expansion is applied only post hoc to trained networks.
Canonical polysemantic neurons are not revisited.
Activation-range cutoffs and explanation scoring are not varied.

missing.what: Feature-capacity fold change for 8-clause nets while varying neuron count, α=2 and 4. Larger gains at small widths bear on V3's feature-to-neuron pressure.
Regression of accuracy gain on capacity fold change across widths, with R² reported.
Accuracy of the Boolean nets in the Table A1 settings (relative improvement across clauses and neurons). This is needed to pair capacity gains with performance.
Expansion factor α used for Table A1 is not stated in the rows.

record.verdict_notes: Polysemanticity is measured only through feature capacity computed from first-layer weights, plus figure-only collision and clause-recovery metrics, all in toy Boolean networks. Dense capacity below the feature count even when neurons outnumber clauses is suggestive for V4, but the authors do not interpret it. It could reflect the dense all-to-all first layer or the L1/L2 regularization used, so V4 is left untested. Real-data experiments have no polysemanticity measure beyond weight cosine similarity.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test individual neurons in image classifiers for strong responses to unrelated image inputs, including the InceptionV1 example.
No transformer language models, MLP-neuron token/context responses, or layerwise language-model comparisons; the paper identifies transformer-scale models as future work.

Tests the feature-collision/superposition account mainly in Boolean DNF networks and related classifier settings. It does not establish that this is the cause of polysemanticity in all trained networks or in language models.
Does not test polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when there is enough capacity for every feature.

Tests fixed-parameter neuron expansion and related sparsity settings, but does not compare SoLU with other activations, systematically vary activation functions or regularization, or test modern convolutional networks for a change in polysemanticity metrics.
Does not revisit canonical polysemantic neurons with improved tools to determine whether their mixed inputs share one natural feature or job.
Does not vary activation-range cutoffs or explanation-scoring procedures to test measurement dependence.

tranche.reason: Different method (fixed-parameter neuron expansion, feature capacity) aimed at superposition and interference in toy Boolean nets.

source_check.notes: 12/24/32/128 literals = 3/6/8/32 clauses; Table A1 does not state α. The l0 condition (3–32 clauses) overlaps l1 (3, 6 clauses); the 3/6-clause sharing bears more directly on V4, which has no verdict. Collision and clause-recovery rows are figure-only (10 trials, called preliminary by the authors); the case study used 1000 epochs.

statements.correction: Table A1 (8 dense neurons, 5 trials): 32 literals (8 clauses) 3.944 ± 0.409 to 6.977 ± 0.426 clause-split; 128 literals (32 clauses) 7.699 ± 1.029 to 16.87 ± 0.926 clause-split. Dense capacity per clause, derived from Table A1 (not stated in text): 0.63 at 3 clauses, about 0.48-0.49 at 6-10, 0.37 at 15, 0.24 at 32. collision-sweep (Fig. A7, figure-only) measures edge-level collision rate, not capacity.
statements.problem: All numbers match Table A1, and literals=32 (8 clauses) and 32 clauses (128 literals) are both labelled correctly. But the per-feature capacity claim is cited to collision-sweep, an edge-collision-rate figure that gives no capacity values. The claim can only be derived from Table A1.
1.896 (12 literals = 3 clauses) and 2.907 (24 literals = 6 clauses) match Table A1 for dense 8-neuron nets. The maxima of 3 and 6 are derived from capacity per clause being at most 1.

Numbers match Table A1. The text gives this study's training budget: dense nets pre-trained 25 epochs (to within 95% of converged performance), then 25 fine-tune epochs. This bears on the under-training comparison.

statements.correction: 2510.04500 trains an MLP on FashionMNIST pixels, MLP heads on frozen CLIP ViT-B/16 embeddings (CIFAR-100, ImageNet-100, ImageNet-1k) and a CNN+MLP on CIFAR-100. On CIFAR-100 CLIP it reports accuracy gains, lower neuron weight cosine similarity after random-split FPE (Fig. 6c), and larger gains with more classes per width (Fig. 6d). It measures no neuron response polysemanticity and does not examine the CLIP encoder's neurons.
statements.problem: It is right that no neuron-level polysemanticity is measured in a vision model. But 'exclude real vision models' misdescribes this study, which trains real-image classifiers and reads its results there through superposition.

1.896 ± 0.377 to 2.740 ± 0.114 (12 literals), 5.584 ± 0.670 to 10.79 ± 0.868 (60 literals), 78.7% to 99.4%/88.7% and five trials all match. The case study compares the dense model and FPE models after equal continued training, with 1000 epochs, unlike the Table A1 runs.

The text defines feature capacity as its measure and calls high capacity indicative of lower polysemanticity. It also uses neuron cosine similarity, edge collision rate and clause recovery, all of them proxies.
